title: CFA Ethics 33: Standard VI(A) - what to disclose, to whom, and where
subtitle: The 'could reasonably be expected to impair' test, and why a footnote does not count as disclosure
whyItMatters: Standard VI(A) is the foundation of the whole VI group, and it uses a broader test than most candidates assume: not which conflicts actually did impair judgement, but which ones could reasonably be expected to.
openingQuestion: You hold 200 shares in a company you are about to write research on. The amount is tiny relative to your income. Do you have to disclose it?
openingOptions: No, the value is too small to influence your judgement
Yes - the conflict could reasonably be expected to matter
Only if the value exceeds a set share of your net worth
Only if you intend to sell the holding in the near future
explanation: The crux is who gets to decide which conflicts are material. Standard VI(A) hands that decision to the reader: your duty is to supply the information so they can judge for themselves, not to judge on their behalf and then stay quiet. The reason is entirely practical - the person inside the conflict is the worst-placed judge of whether their own interest is bending their judgement. The disclosure must also be prominent and comprehensible: a line of small print in the footer, or a paragraph in legal language the average reader does not follow, fails the 'full and meaningful disclosure' test.

summary.keyIdea: Disclosure exists so the recipient can judge for themselves, so it only means anything when it reaches the right person, at the right time, in a place they actually read.
summary.commonMistake: Disclosing where nobody reads. A line of small print at the end of the report is technically disclosure and, in terms of its purpose, is not.

application.title: Three questions
application.message: What to disclose, to whom, and where. The third question decides whether the first two mean anything at all.

sections.text: Standard VI(A) requires disclosure of every conflict of interest that could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity. Three details inside that sentence govern the whole of how it is applied.
The test is 'could impair', not 'did impair'
You do not have to prove the conflict actually bent your judgement. It is enough that it belongs to the class of things an ordinary person would want to know before reading your recommendation.

sections.label: Who judges materiality
sections.text: The reader, not the person holding the conflict. Your duty is to supply the information so they can judge for themselves, not to judge on their behalf and then keep quiet. The reason is entirely practical: the person inside the conflict is the worst-placed judge of whether their own interest is bending their judgement.

It has to be prominent and comprehensible. A line of small print in the footer, or a paragraph of legal language the average reader does not follow, does not meet the standard of full and meaningful disclosure - in form it does, in purpose it does not.

Two separate duties are often collapsed into one: disclosure to your employer and disclosure to your clients. Telling one does not stand in for telling the other, because the two use the information for different purposes. And the correct sequence is still to avoid the conflict first and disclose what cannot be avoided - disclosure is not a licence to leave the conflict in place.

lines: Disclosure does not make a conflict disappear.
It simply gives the reader back the right to decide how far to trust you.

diagram.label: The test: could reasonably be expected to impair
The reader judges materiality, not you
Disclosure must be prominent and comprehensible
A footer in legal language does not meet the test

realWorldExample.company: Disclosure to the employer and to the client are two different duties
realWorldExample.description: Standard VI(A) requires disclosure to both, and the content is not the same. To the employer: anything that could affect your independence and objectivity, so that they can manage the conflict at an institutional level. To clients and prospective clients: anything that could affect the objectivity of the recommendation they are receiving. A conflict reported to the firm but never mentioned to the client is still an unmet duty.

quiz.question: What is the test for which conflicts have to be disclosed?
options: A conflict that actually changed the report's conclusion
A conflict that could reasonably be expected to sway judgement
A conflict whose value exceeds the firm's own internal threshold
A conflict the regulator requires to be filed periodically
quiz.explanation: The test is deliberately broad: if you wait until a bent judgement can be demonstrated, it will essentially never be demonstrated. A firm's own monetary threshold cannot be the boundary either, because it is set by the party with the incentive to set it high, and a regulatory filing schedule covers a narrow list of interests rather than everything a reader would reasonably want to know before weighing your work.

quiz.question: Who decides how material a conflict is?
options: The firm's compliance team, following its internal procedure
The analyst, since they understand the situation best
The reader of the report, using the information you give
The regulator, during a periodic inspection visit
quiz.explanation: The person inside the conflict is the worst-placed judge of whether their own interest is bending their judgement, which is exactly why the Standard moves the decision to the reader. Compliance has a role in managing conflicts at the institutional level, but that is a different job from the reader's own assessment, and a regulator arriving for an inspection comes far too late to help anyone acting on the report today.

quiz.question: Does a footer in legal language meet the disclosure standard?
options: No, unless the report also carries a separate summary
Yes, as long as the wording is complete and accurate
Yes, if the readers are all professional investors instead
No - disclosure must be prominent and easy to understand
quiz.explanation: A disclosure the reader neither notices nor understands has communicated nothing, so the form of it is part of the duty rather than a presentational afterthought. Completeness and accuracy are necessary but not sufficient. And a professional audience does not lower the bar: sophistication tells you what vocabulary is safe to use, not whether the disclosure may be buried where nobody looks.

quiz.question: How do disclosure to your employer and disclosure to your client differ?
options: Two separate duties; meeting one does not meet the other
Tell the employer only; they will pass it on to clients
Tell the client only, since they are the affected party
The same duty, so a single disclosure discharges both at once
quiz.explanation: The employer needs to know so it can manage the conflict at an institutional level; the client needs to know so they can assess the recommendation they are being handed. Because the two use the information for different purposes, neither disclosure substitutes for the other, and assuming the firm will relay it downstream leaves the duty resting on a step nobody has actually agreed to take.

quiz.question: Why is the 'could reasonably be expected' test broader than an 'actually impaired' test?
options: Because regulators want to collect more disclosure data
Because a skewed judgement can almost never actually be proved
Because a narrower test would make research reports too long
Because every conflict of interest genuinely does skew judgement
quiz.explanation: A standard that only bites once influence can be demonstrated would in practice almost never bite at all, since nobody can show what an unconflicted version of the same analyst would have concluded. The point is not that every conflict does distort - many do not - nor is it about report length or the volume of data reaching a regulator. It is about which conflicts are ever caught.

keyTakeaways: The test is 'could reasonably be expected to impair', not 'did impair'
The reader judges materiality, not the person holding the conflict
Disclosure must be prominent and comprehensible - a legal footer fails
Disclosure to the employer and to the client are two separate duties
Avoid the conflict first; disclose the part that cannot be avoided

practicePrompt.question: Your firm is underwriting an issue for company X, and you have been asked to write research on X. How do you handle it?
options: Write it as normal since you personally have no stake in the deal
Disclose the underwriting relationship prominently in the report
Decline to write the report; the conflict cannot be cured
Write it and send the draft to company X for review first
practicePrompt.explanation: The conflict here belongs to the institution rather than to you personally, and that does not soften the duty - which is exactly where the first option goes wrong. Two things have to happen together: disclose it so the reader knows, and check the internal rules, since many firms restrict research publication during an underwriting period. Sending a draft to the subject of the analysis creates a fresh independence breach of its own.
